conventions.convention: Inner products are linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second.
The singular values of T:V→W are the eigenvalues, with multiplicity and in weakly decreasing order, of |T|=sqrt(T* T); zero singular values are retained.
The operator norm is defined as 0 when the domain V is zero; otherwise it is the maximum of ||Tv|| over unit vectors.

The Riemann-to-Lebesgue comparison is stated under Countable Choice, and measurability of the original function—not merely an almost-everywhere Borel representative—uses completeness of Lebesgue measure.
For right-continuous nondecreasing F, the comparison uses the Lebesgue–Stieltjes measure convention μ_F((u,v])=F(v)−F(u), so the matching measure integral is over (a,b].
A cycle admissible for the residue theorem is null-homologous in the ambient open set and its trace avoids the pole set of the meromorphic function.
Zero and pole counts on a cycle are weighted both by local order and by the winding number n(Γ,a), rather than being unweighted counts of interior points.

A plurisubharmonic function is upper semicontinuous, is not identically −∞ on a component of the ambient domain, and restricts on each affine complex line component to a subharmonic function or the identically −∞ function.
The boundary-radius function δ_Ω uses equal-radius open polydiscs, equivalently sup-norm distance to the complement; for a set E it is written as inf_{a∈E} δ_Ω(a).
Hartogs pseudoconvexity means specifically that −log δ_Ω is plurisubharmonic; a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion is real-valued and has compact sublevel sets in Ω.
Levi pseudoconvexity uses a defining function negative on the domain and tests semipositivity only on complex tangent vectors satisfying ∂ρ(p)·v=0.

load_bearing.statement: For a domain Ω⊆C^m, the following are equivalent: Ω is a domain of holomorphy; every compact K⊂⊂Ω satisfies δ_Ω(hat K_Ω)=δ_Ω(K); and Ω is holomorphically convex.
Let V be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and T:V→V linear. Then T is normal if and only if V has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of T.

For T:V→W between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces, if r is the number of positive singular values, there are orthonormal bases (e_j) and (f_j) with Tv=Σ_{j=1}^r s_j⟨v,e_j⟩f_j and s_1≥⋯≥s_r>0.
Assuming Countable Choice, a bounded Riemann-integrable f:[a,b]→R with integral I admits bounded Borel φ≤f≤ψ whose Lebesgue integrals both equal I; in particular ∫(ψ−φ)=0.
Assuming Countable Choice, a bounded Riemann-integrable f:[a,b]→R is Lebesgue measurable and integrable and satisfies ∫_[a,b] f dλ_1=∫_a^b f(x) dx.
For meromorphic f and an admissible cycle Γ on whose trace f has no zero, (2πi)^{-1}∫_Γ f'/f=Z(f,Γ)−P(f,Γ), with only finitely many nonzero terms.
If γ is a closed contour null-homologous in Ω, f and g are holomorphic on Ω, and |f−g|<|g| on γ*, then f and g have the same weighted number of zeros with respect to γ.

A function u:Ω→[−∞,∞) is plurisubharmonic when it is upper semicontinuous, is not identically −∞ on a component of Ω, and every nonconstant affine-line restriction is subharmonic or identically −∞ on each line-domain component.

If Ω is a domain of holomorphy and a continuous family of analytic discs has every boundary circle in one compact K⊂⊂Ω and its initial closed disc compactly contained in Ω, then every closed disc in the family lies in Ω.
For a self-adjoint T on an n-dimensional real inner product space with λ_1≥⋯≥λ_n, λ_k=min_{dim W=n−k+1} max_{0≠v∈W}R_T(v)=max_{dim U=k} min_{0≠v∈U}R_T(v).

published_dependencies.used_for: Fixes the linear-first inner-product convention used throughout the spectral and SVD pages.
Defines adjoints by the identity ⟨Tv,w⟩=⟨v,T*w⟩ and explicitly separates definition from existence.
Supplies existence and uniqueness of adjoints for finite-dimensional maps, including zero spaces.
Supplies additivity, conjugate scalar-linearity, reversal of products, and the double-adjoint identity.
Makes spectral and Jordan primary projections polynomials in the operator.
Makes the splitting field in the Jordan–Chevalley construction separable over the perfect base field.
Relates conjugate roots through base-field automorphisms in the attempted Jordan–Chevalley descent.
Turns bounds by 1/n into zero-integral conclusions in the Darboux-envelope argument.
Produces partitions with arbitrarily small upper-minus-lower Darboux gap.
Preserves Darboux-gap bounds under common refinement.
Derives Arzelà bounded convergence from Lebesgue bounded convergence.
Supplies completeness of Lebesgue measure and measurability of subsets of null sets.
Tests Riemann integrability of the examples by the Lebesgue measure of their discontinuity sets.
Fixes meromorphic functions as complex-valued holomorphic functions off a discrete pole set.
Defines finite zero order and assigns order +∞ when every Taylor coefficient vanishes.
Fixes pole avoidance and null-homology for residue and argument-principle cycles.
Defines cycle integrals and winding indices, including the empty-chain convention.
Relates pole order, reciprocal zero behavior, divergence of modulus, and finite principal parts.
Converts indexed residues into contour integrals in the argument principles.
Fixes the simultaneous-extension-pair convention for domains of holomorphy.
Supplies extension from a standard Hartogs figure to its bidisc hull.
Produces the real-linear separator converted into a complex-linear functional.
Fixes upper-semicontinuity, the nontriviality condition, and the disc-submean convention.
Provides the one-variable maximum principle invoked on affine complex lines.
Converts nonnegative one-variable Laplacian into subharmonicity in the Levi criterion.
Controls decreasing limits on every affine complex line.
Controls locally upper-bounded suprema after upper-semicontinuous regularization.
Provides harmonic comparison used in the linewise pseudoconvexity argument.
Bounds mixed derivatives on compact sets before propagation to holomorphic hulls.
Supplies convergent expansions on strictly smaller polydiscs.
Computes the product-torus hull via the distinguished boundary maximum principle.

concerns.concern: Step 1.1 defines each envelope using a sum over i<m_n−1 and then assigns the last interval coefficient only at {b}. The entire half-open interval [t_{m_n−1},b) is omitted. For f≡1 the asserted upper envelope is 0 there, so f≤u_n and the Darboux-sum integral identities both fail.

In the proof of holomorphic convexity ⇒ domain of holomorphy, a single strict inequality |g_n(p_n)|>sup_{K_n}|g_n| does not permit scalar rescaling to make the value at p_n arbitrarily large while making the supremum on K_n arbitrarily small; the ratio is invariant under scaling. Powers or another separation-amplification construction are required. The later claim that the infinite tail cannot cancel at p_n also needs a nested diagonal construction not stated here.

Step 1.2 asserts that an arbitrary continuous family of analytic discs locally sweeps out a standard Hartogs figure whose bidisc hull crosses the boundary. No nondegeneracy or local-surjectivity hypothesis supports that assertion, and deriving a Hartogs figure from a possibly constant or highly degenerate family is the substantive continuity-principle argument, not an immediate coordinate change.

Step 1.1 says −log(−ρ) agrees with −log δ_Ω “up to a smooth local norm comparison” and therefore inherits plurisubharmonicity. Bounded or smooth comparability does not preserve plurisubharmonicity, so the displayed Levi-form argument has no established semipositivity premise. Moreover, tangency only at p does not by itself make the squared-gradient term vanish along an arbitrary interior approach.

Step 5.1 makes two essential descent assertions without a cited or proved fixed-field theorem: that automorphism-fixed scalar-extended operators descend to V over F, and that an automorphism-fixed residue class modulo the minimal polynomial has an F[x] representative. The preceding conjugacy result does not supply either conclusion.

The remark says the next lemma shows that the singularities at zeros and poles are always simple. The definition permits the holomorphic function f≡0, for which f'/f is defined nowhere, every point has infinite zero order, and there is no isolated simple pole to which the lemma applies.

For f≡0 and the empty admissible cycle, every index is 0 and the stated finiteness condition is satisfied, but every zero has order +∞ under the cited convention. The displayed sum therefore contains undefined products 0·(+∞), so the definition and the argument-principle theorem that consumes it need a nonzero-function or finite-order hypothesis.

The definition gives δ_Ω(E)=inf_{a∈E}δ_Ω(a) for every E⊆Ω but supplies neither an extended-real codomain nor a convention for inf ∅. The empty-set case used by later hull statements is therefore undefined.

Step 3.1 says an arbitrary orthonormal complex eigenbasis “splits into” real eigenvectors and conjugate pairs. Conjugation maps E_λ isometrically to E_conj(λ), but an independently chosen orthonormal basis of the latter need not consist of the conjugates of the selected basis of E_λ. A conjugation-compatible basis choice and the orthogonality between the resulting real planes must be constructed.

Steps 2.1 and 3.1 use the false implication W∩U={0} ⇒ W⊆U⊥. The needed nontrivial intersections follow instead from the dimension formula dim(W∩U)≥dim W+dim U−n. Replacing those two sentences repairs the proof, but the inference as written is invalid.

After proving u is constant on one ball, step 2.1 claims {u=u(a)} is open by the same local-maximum argument and closed by upper semicontinuity. Away from the initial ball, a point with value u(a) need not be a local maximum, and an equality level set of an upper-semicontinuous function need not be closed without a global upper bound. The strong maximum principle is true, but propagation requires a separate line-chain argument.

Step 1.2 summarizes the cited power-series theorem more strongly than it is stated: the source expands a continuous separately holomorphic function on a polydisc only on strictly smaller polydiscs. A reader can recover the intended Taylor-radius conclusion from the derivative bounds by inserting intermediate radii, but that argument is absent.

Steps 1.1–1.2 infer closure(Δ_r(a))⊆Ω directly from Δ_r(a)⊆Ω. What is needed is to choose r′ with r<r′<δ_Ω(K); then closure(Δ_r(a))⊆Δ_r′(a)⊆Ω and the cited Cauchy estimate applies with a strictly larger polydisc.

Part 3 invokes a “cited one-variable source result” that convex nondecreasing composition preserves subharmonicity, but the only listed one-variable dependency covers positive linear combinations and finite maxima. The claim is standard, yet its actual supporting theorem or a Jensen/submean derivation is missing.

Step 1.1 falsely says that because f is not identically zero on Ω, its restriction to every affine-line component is not identically zero. For example f(z_1,z_2)=z_1 vanishes identically on the line z_1=0. The conclusion survives because the definition explicitly permits an identically −∞ line restriction, but the proof must handle that branch.

When V≠0 but T=0 (in particular when W=0), the proof has r=0 and nevertheless refers to f_1 and the equation Te_1=σ_1f_1. There is no first left-singular vector in a zero codomain. The zero-operator case is immediate but must be separated before step 2.1.

The Statement first requires S:V→V to be a global linear isometry, then calls this “equivalent” to S being an isometry only on (ker T)⊥=im U. The latter is strictly weaker for singular T and is the usual partial-isometry formulation. The existence proof constructs a global extension, but the equivalence sentence conflates the two formulations.

Step 2.1 proves J(t) is integer-valued only for real t∈[0,1], then calls J an integer-valued holomorphic function on the whole complex disc. The conclusion is repairable: continuity makes J constant on [0,1], or the identity theorem applies after fixing that constant on the interval. That intermediate argument is missing.

The example is a valid counterexample because f=z+1 has zero interior zeros while g=z has one, but step 2.1 instead says the interior zero-count conclusion is “not well posed” merely because f has a boundary zero. Counting zeros in the open unit disc remains well defined; it is the logarithmic-derivative contour formula that becomes unavailable.
